reason: 'Radiant' petals in umbels mean outer petals enlarged and pointing outward. Radiating and radiant are different things, and the PATO term may be about radial pattern. A rule would need to map 'radiant' to enlarged or outward-pointing outer petals.
A swollen ovary is meaningful, and the examples fit.
A striate seed coat is a normal sculpture. The examples are correct.

The examples are not about presence. They give valve length, a hooked apex and how the fruit opens, so this pair comes from a wrong reading. Presence belongs to the presence pattern, not to this pair.
Leaf scars can be convex, and the examples say so.
Pyrenes (stones) can be pointed at one or both ends. This is a shape of the ends of the pyrene.
A viscidium can be hyaline. Hyaline is read as transparent, which is close enough here.

Entire describes a margin or apex, not the whole glume. The examples (apex entire, wing margin entire) are about those sub-parts. A rule would need to send 'entire' to the margin or apex, and keep the pair for the glume only when the glume margin is meant.
A corolla tube can be wide or widened.
A cupule enclosing a nut is a standard description (Fagaceae).
A calyptra can be split (cleft). The examples fit, including the negated one.
A connective can be enlarged or broadened.
A sporocarp can be elliptic in outline.
Shoots and stems can be hollow.
Tepals can be translucent. The 'pellucid glands' example is a wrong reading of a gland, but the other examples are correct.
The count of segments or articles belongs to the loment as the whole, using the counted-parts pattern. Counting segments on the segment itself is a wrong bearer.
Drupes fused to each other is meaningful (multiple fruits).
A pedicel can be small or minute. The 'prickles' example is a different part but does not change the pair.
Stipule lobes can be linear.
The examples are about tertiary veins (nervures), not vascular bundles. The bearer is wrong. The right part is the leaf vein.
A ligule can be rudimentary or obsolete.
Calyx lobes can be serrate.
Leaf lobes can be tomentose.
Sepals can be woody (ligneous) as they thicken in fruit.
Chestnut brown stipules are a normal colour description.
Labellum lobes can be acuminate. The 'apiculate' examples are a close apex shape.
The examples say rounded at apex, which is a shape of the berry apex, not the whole berry. Obtuse also differs from rounded. A rule would need to send apex shape to the berry apex.
Staminodes can be rectangular.
A corolla limb has a width, and the examples are measurements.
A lamina can be falcate (sickle-shaped).
Pappus bristles can be plumose (feathery).
A leaf apex can be thickened.
It is the areoles that are hexagonal, not the veinlets. The veinlets only form them. The bearer is wrong (areole, or the venation pattern).
Follicles can be hairy or glabrous. Pilosity is the attribute.
Labellum lobes can have a crenate margin, which is read as scalloped. The examples are about margins, so the margin may be the more exact bearer, but the pair is fine.
A leaf sheath can have a rough texture.
The examples are about glands or glandular hairs on the leaves of the short shoot, not the shoot itself. A rule would need to tell the glands on the shoot from glands on its leaves.
Seed coat or testa with fibres (fibrillose) is meaningful.
Scale leaves can be pubescent.
A whole plant can be sticky (glutinous).
A floral disc can be velvety.
A leaf margin can be irregular. Examples about irregular width are a different thing, but most examples fit.
Stipules can clasp or encircle the stem.
The cell dimensions are given as length × width, so width is meaningful. The bearer is probably a hair or filament cell in the source, so it deserves a spot check.
Peristome teeth can be nodulose. Some examples are about cilia, but the pair itself is fine.
The examples describe an alar region that is poorly defined, not an alar cell that is inconspicuous. The bearer is wrong (region, not cell).
Epidermal cells can be small.
Peristome teeth can be blunt.
Bulbils have a length, and the examples are measurements in µm.
'Capsules mature mid-summer' gives a season, not a ripeness state. It belongs to a phenology rule, not to a capsule quality.
An androphore can be long, and the examples are measurements.
A cyme can be short.
A dorsal radicle (incumbent) is about its position against the cotyledons, which needs a second entity. A rule would need to say whether this relational term is accepted for the radicle.
An aril can be oblique.
Legumes can be held obliquely, and 'obliques' also describes their shape.
A staminal tube can be truncated at the top.
Entire is a margin term. 'Entières' most likely describes leaf or lobe margins, so this pair comes from a wrong reading.
Berries can be hairy.
Sepals can be persistent or caducous.
Secondary veins can be branched or forked.
